paragraphs: Marrowby is a small harbour town on the northern coast of the Grey Sea. It was founded in 1742 by salt traders who needed a safe place to dry their nets, and the town grew quickly after the new pier opened in 1810.

The town is known for its narrow streets (most of them paved with dark granite) and for a market that sells smoked fish every Thursday. Visitors often say the harbour feels "older than the sea itself" when the fog comes in.
Mr. Smith, the first harbour master, kept a diary of every ship. His diary survives in the town library. Historians still read it today, and the library lends copies to schools.

sections.title: History
paragraphs: During the war years of 1914-1918 the harbour was closed to fishing boats. The fishing families moved inland, and many of them never came back to the coast. The harbour reopened in 1921 with only 12 boats.
The harbour council rebuilt the harbour wall in 1956 after a storm destroyed the old one. The new wall is 340 metres long, and the harbour lights were moved to its northern end.
Today the harbour hosts a festival every summer. Fishermen race their boats across the bay, children paint the old buoys, and the evening ends with music on the pier.

sections.title: Daily life
paragraphs: The boats come back at noon. The nets are full of herring. Children run down to the pier. The gulls follow them all the way.
Market stalls open early. Bakers sell warm bread before dawn. The church bell rings twice. Then the streets go quiet again.
Winter brings long nights. Storms close the harbour for days. Families gather around their stoves and tell old stories.

sections.title: Landmarks
paragraphs: The harbour's old quay (built of grey granite in the time of the salt traders) still stands. The keeper's cottage (now a small museum) sits at its end.
Children's games on the quay (mostly races and hide and seek) fill the summer evenings. The town's oldest inn faces the water.
